summary: Defines a BGP Outbound Route Filter type called the Covering Prefixes ORF. A router can use it to ask a neighbor to send only routes that cover certain prefixes. It is useful in virtual hub-and-spoke VPNs and in BGP/MPLS Ethernet VPN networks.

eli5.summary: A shop tells its supplier, only send me the catalogs that cover the things I actually sell. Less paper arrives, so less needs filing.

questions: what is a bgp outbound route filter
subtitle: A BGP route filter a router can send to pull only the routes that cover one host address.

tldr.problem: In virtual hub-and-spoke VPNs and in EVPN, a spoke router starts with only a default route toward a hub, but sometimes wants a more direct route to one specific host or MAC address.
tldr.mechanism: The spoke sends a ROUTE-REFRESH message with a Covering Prefixes ORF (type 65) naming a host address. The peer selects the most specific matching route, tags it with an import route target and advertises it.
tldr.outcome: A spoke can pull just the routes it needs, on demand, instead of receiving everything. Each CP-ORF costs memory and compute on the device, so peers should be trusted and limited.

today: RFC 7543 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2015, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Pulling Routes on Demand
sections.content:
A BGP speaker can send Outbound Route Filters (ORFs, RFC 5291) to a peer. The peer uses them to filter the routing updates it sends back, which gives a 'route pull' model where routes are fetched on demand.

RFC 7543 defines a new ORF type, the Covering Prefixes ORF (CP-ORF). A speaker sends it to pull routes that cover a given host address. A prefix covers a host address if it can be used to forward traffic toward that address. The document says CP-ORF is applicable in Virtual Hub-and-Spoke VPNs (RFC 7024, RFC 4364) and in BGP/MPLS Ethernet VPN (EVPN, RFC 7432) networks.
sections.eli5: Instead of getting every map, you ask: 'which maps include this one house?' and only those arrive.

sections.title: CP-ORF Encoding
sections.content:
CP-ORF entries ride inside the BGP ROUTE-REFRESH message defined by RFC 5291. When it carries CP-ORF entries, the ORF Type MUST be 65, the Match field MUST be PERMIT, and the AFI/SAFI pair MUST be either IPv4 or IPv6 with MPLS-labeled VPN address, or L2VPN with BGP EVPN.

The type-specific part has a 32-bit Sequence (the entry's position among CP-ORFs), 8-bit Minlen and Maxlen, a 64-bit VPN Route Target to match, a 64-bit Import Route Target to add, an 8-bit Route Type, and a Host Address of 0, 32, 48 or 128 bits.

Further rules depend on the AFI. For IPv4, Minlen and Maxlen MUST be at most 32 with Minlen no larger than Maxlen, Route Type MUST be 0, and the host address is exactly 32 bits. IPv6 is the same with 128. For L2VPN, Route Type is an EVPN route type from 1 to 4. For types 1, 3 and 4, Minlen and Maxlen MUST be 0 and the host address absent. For type 2 (MAC/IP Advertisement), the lengths are at most 48 and the host address is exactly 48 bits.
sections.eli5: The request is a form: which group of routes, how specific, which address you care about, and what label to stick on the answers.

sections.title: Processing Rules
sections.content:
If a ROUTE-REFRESH message with a CP-ORF breaks any encoding rule, the receiver MUST ignore the whole message and SHOULD log it. Otherwise it handles each entry by its Action: ADD inserts the entry into the peer's Outbound Filter at the position given by Sequence, REMOVE deletes it, and REMOVE-ALL clears all CP-ORF entries.

When filtering, the speaker evaluates CP-ORF entries before other entries. For IPv4-VPN and IPv6-VPN routes, a route matches only if it carries the VPN Route Target, its prefix length lies between Minlen and Maxlen (each plus 64 bits for the Route Distinguisher), its leading bits match the host address for Minlen bits, and Loc-RIB holds no more specific route that also meets the conditions. Route Distinguishers are ignored when comparing prefixes.

The RFC works an example with Minlen 1, Maxlen 32 and host address 192.0.2.1. Of the routes 1:0.0.0.0/64, 2:192.0.2.0/88 and 3:192.0.2.0/89, only the last matches, because the first is too short and the second has a more specific covering route.

A matching route goes into the Adj-RIB-Out with the Import Route Target added to its route targets and a Transitive Opaque Extended Community with sub-type CP-ORF (0x03). Removing entries can cause previously advertised routes to be withdrawn. For a message with only CP-ORF entries, the speaker MUST re-advertise affected routes and it is RECOMMENDED not to re-advertise unaffected ones.
sections.eli5: The helper keeps the most detailed map that still covers your house, stamps it with your chosen label, and sends it. If a request is malformed, it throws the whole request away.

sections.title: Virtual Hub-and-Spoke VPN Use
sections.content:
In a virtual hub-and-spoke VPN, a PE router is a V-hub, a V-spoke or neither. The RFC's example has V-spoke1, V-hub1, a PE called PE1 and a route reflector (RR). V-hub1 advertises a VPN-IP default route carrying RT-RED-FROM-HUB1. V-spoke1 signals interest in that route target through a Route Target Membership NLRI (RFC 4684) and receives the default route, so all its traffic goes through the hub.

When V-spoke1 decides a flow would benefit from a more direct route to host H, it numbers H and sends a ROUTE-REFRESH to the RR with a CP-ORF: Minlen 1, Maxlen 32 or 128, VPN Route Target RT-RED, Import Route Target RT-RED-FROM-HUB1, and Host Address H. The RR makes sure it has all the VPN's routes, adds the CP-ORF to the filter, and advertises the covering prefix P to V-spoke1 with next hop PE1. V-spoke1 accepts it because of the added route target. How a spoke decides it needs a direct route is outside the document.

For Multicast VPN, routes carrying the CP-ORF community MUST NOT be used to determine Eligible Upstream Multicast Hops.
sections.eli5: A spoke normally sends everything through the hub. When it wants a shortcut to one house, it asks the post office for just that route.

sections.title: EVPN Use
sections.content:
In EVPN, a PE for an EVPN instance acts as a Default MAC Gateway (DMG), a Spoke, or neither. A DMG advertises an Unknown MAC Route (UMR), a MAC/IP Advertisement route with MAC address length set to 0 in the example. A spoke first sends one ROUTE-REFRESH with four CP-ORF entries, with Sequence 1 to 4, one for each EVPN route type (1 Ethernet Autodiscovery, 2 MAC/IP Advertisement, 3 Inclusive Multicast, 4 Ethernet Segment), all with Minlen and Maxlen 0. The RR then sends the matching routes, including the DMG's UMR.

Later, if the spoke wants a more direct path to MAC address M, it sends a CP-ORF with Route Type 2, Minlen 1, Maxlen 48 and Host Address M. In this case the RR does not change the route targets on the routes it sends; it only adds the CP-ORF community. If an EVI has several DMGs, the spoke follows its local route selection to choose the best UMR.
sections.eli5: Same idea for Ethernet networks: the spoke first asks for the basics, then asks for the shortcut to one particular device by its hardware address.

sections.title: Resource Limits and Security
sections.content:
Each CP-ORF uses memory and compute resources on the device. The RFC therefore says that BGP speakers periodically evaluate the CP-ORFs they originated and remove unneeded ones, using local policy to decide which.

To avoid oversubscription, a device supporting CP-ORF advertises willingness to receive it only to known, trusted iBGP peers when negotiating the ORF capability, and enforces a per-peer limit on installed CP-ORFs, ignoring requests beyond the limit. General BGP security is covered by RFC 4271 and RFC 6952.
sections.eli5: Every special request takes some of the helper's time and memory, so only trusted friends may ask, and there is a cap on how many each can make.

sections.title: Code Points
sections.content: RFC 7543 uses code points from the First Come First Served range of two registries: CP-ORF is 65 in the BGP Outbound Route Filtering (ORF) Types registry, and CP-ORF is 0x03 in the Transitive Opaque Extended Community Sub-Types registry. IANA updated those entries to reference this document.
sections.eli5: The RFC reserved two labels, 65 and 0x03, so everybody uses the same ones.

fields.name: Minlen
fields.desc: Minimum length of the selected route, in bits.

fields.name: Maxlen
fields.desc: Maximum length of the selected route, in bits.

fields.name: VPN Route Target
fields.desc: Route target the selected route must carry.

fields.name: Import Route Target
fields.desc: Route target added to the advertised route.
